headline: High: Flowise’s broad network/filesystem/tooling can amplify prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when paired with a non-runnable docs-only agent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is non-runnable and has no shared channel or I/O surface, so it cannot directly ingest Agent B’s outputs. Agent B can read/write files and run browsers, but the pair lacks a documented bridge beyond manual transfer, making prompt injection possible only through unusual operator copy-paste or file handoff.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies B-generated content into A-facing prompts or files, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared workspace is introduced outside the profiles, the pathway strengthens.
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces.
Avoid copy-pasting B outputs into A prompts.
Strip instructions from any transferred text.
Use a fixed template for handoffs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on transferred artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B touches chatflow inputs/outputs, files, and broad network egress, while Agent A is docs-only and touches no data classes. If A is used as a source of content that B stores or forwards, B can leak that material through its default file and network surfaces; the pair’s interaction is not documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF A is supplied with sensitive text and B persists or forwards it, leakage occurs.
IF B is configured with external model providers or HTTP tools, content can leave the workspace.
mitigations: Do not route sensitive inputs through B.
Disable external HTTP/model tools for sensitive runs.
Use redacted test data.
Review uploaded files before execution.
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters on B egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A has no write or execution capability, but Agent B can write files and shares state across instances via server datastore. If A’s outputs are materialized into B-managed files or flows, B can overwrite or race with other B instances. The conflict is one-sided, yet the shared mutable backend makes the interaction plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF multiple B instances operate on the same datastore, write races can occur.
IF A-derived artifacts are stored in B-managed files, later B runs may overwrite them.
mitigations: Assign unique run IDs per flow.
Separate per-run directories.
Lock shared datastore writes.
Avoid storing A outputs in mutable B state.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency controls.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B is a graph-based orchestrator that can treat upstream content as tool inputs, while Agent A provides no verification or execution layer. If A’s outputs are fed into B flows, B may act on them without independent validation, creating a default cascading-error path even though A itself is non-runnable.
conditions: IF A-generated text is used as an input node in B, downstream actions may follow unverified facts.
IF B flows include email, HTTP, or file-write tools, errors can propagate outward.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before action nodes.
Require human approval for outbound actions.
Use schema validation on A outputs.
Limit B to read-only dry runs.
requires-engineering: add confidence gates between nodes.

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, EU PII, or residency-sensitive data class is declared for A, so a compliance breach is not evidenced. B does handle chatflow inputs/outputs and secrets, but the profiles do not show a specific residency or certification mismatch between the pair; only a narrow compliance gap is plausible if sensitive data is introduced.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into B and stored outside required residency, a breach may occur.
IF deployment policy requires retention controls that are absent, compliance risk increases.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in B.
Minimize retention of chatflow logs.
Rotate exposed secrets promptly.
Document data residency for deployments.
requires-engineering: implement retention and residency controls.
